chunks: "I'd first say which impedance I mean, since there are three.

The characteristic impedance of the line, Z 0 , is basically flat with frequency: above roughly 10 megahertz on a PCB trace it sits at square root of L' over C' , so 50 ohms stays 50 ohms out to many GHz, with only a small drift from loss and dispersion.
At low frequency, where the resistance matters, Z 0 is larger and has a phase, which is the RC regime.
What does vary a lot is the input impedance you see looking into a finite piece of line.
For a line of electrical length theta equals 2 pi f t d with a load Z L , Z in equals Z 0 the quantity Z L plus jZ 0 theta over the quantity Z 0 plus jZ L theta .
If the line is matched, Z in equals Z 0 at every frequency.
If it isn't, Z in oscillates with frequency, and an open line looks like a capacitor at low frequency, a short at the quarter-wave frequency, an open at the half-wave frequency, and so on.
For a 10 cm FR-4 trace that quarter-wave point is around 415 megahertz.
If the question means insertion loss, that rises steadily with frequency, roughly square root of f from conductor plus f from dielectric, with ripple from reflections if there's a mismatch."
